newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco firms said to agree to cut sales to youths.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco firms said to agree to cut sales to youths.

text.p: Tobacco companies have agreed to cut cigarette sales to teen-agers by 60 percent in the next decade or face huge fines as part of a deal aimed at settling smoking liability issues, The Dallas Morning News reported Saturday.
While negotiations on a broader agreement were continuing, the newspaper said the tobacco industry had agreed with government and private lawyers on a timetable to reduce teen smoking.

It cited Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, a central figure in the talks, as saying the goal was to cut smoking among teen-agers by 30 percent in five years, 50 percent in seven years and 60 percent in 10 years.
He said tobacco companies would be fined for each percentage point they fell short of the targets, and that the fines "could quickly add up to billions and billions of dollars".

The agreement also specified that tobacco firms pay $500 million per year for anti-smoking advertising and end all marketing to teen-agers with character advertising such as Joe Camel and Marlboro Man, The Dallas Morning News said.

It would also bring a ban on billboard advertising and the removal of vending machines in places that allow access to minors, as well as require tobacco companies to sell youth dance clubs they own across the country.
Retailers would be obliged to pay a licensing fee for cigarettes, stock them behind their counters and pay fines if they sold tobacco products to minors.
The newspaper said the provisions on teen smoking were negotiated over the last several days in New York and that a full settlement package would take at least two more weeks of talks.
Congress would have to pass laws authorizing some of the proposed settlement provisions.

Tobacco company lawyers have been in negotiations with 29 state attorneys general, plaintiffs' lawyers and public health advocates for more than two months in search of a deal that would require a big payout from the industry and new government regulations on the manufacture and marketing of cigarettes.
In return, the tobacco companies would be better protected against lawsuits from future class-action lawsuits by smokers seeking punitive damages for health problems.
